tagline: A capital that turns its back on a bay it could ride — where Howth, Dalkey and Dún Laoghaire are minutes apart by water but a slow DART or a clogged road by land.
summary: Dublin Bay strings the city's waterfront from the Docklands out to Dún Laoghaire, Howth, Dalkey and Killiney — coastal villages and headlands that are slow by DART and road at peak but minutes apart by sea. There is effectively no scheduled passenger water transport on the bay today; the city simply doesn't use it. Bolt is a major ride-hail player in Dublin, and a clean foiling tier would turn the bay into a fast commuter and leisure spine — a genuinely new mode for one of Europe's most congested capitals.
competitive_landscape: Unlike most of Navier's European markets, Dublin Bay has almost no on-water passenger transport to displace — just seasonal island boats to Ireland's Eye and Dalkey Island and the cross-Irish-Sea car-ferries from Dublin Port. The absence is the point: the bay is wide, sheltered and ringed by affluent coastal suburbs, yet road and rail are the only links. With Bolt already owning the urban ride-hail relationship, a foiling water tier is a clean greenfield mode rather than a fight over existing ferries.

demand_signals.label: DART coastal commuter corridor
demand_signals.note: The Dublin coastal rail line from Howth to Bray runs at capacity at peak, paralleling a bay that carries no commuter boats — a large, proven coastal travel demand with no water option.

demand_signals.label: Howth & Dalkey leisure villages
demand_signals.note: Affluent coastal villages with marinas, seafood and headland walks draw heavy weekend visitor flows that crawl out by road and rail.

demand_signals.note: The Silicon-Docks tech and financial cluster on the Liffey quays is a dense waterfront workplace with no water-commute option to the coastal suburbs its workforce lives in.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire bay mesh — Docklands↔Dún Laoghaire (~6.5 nm), Howth (~7 nm), Dalkey/Killiney (~9 nm), Dún Laoghaire↔Howth (~7 nm) and the short island hops to Ireland's Eye (~1 nm) and Dalkey Island (~0.3 nm) — sits well inside the 70 nm all-electric range, ideal for a high-frequency clean commuter spine off existing harbours.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The cross-Irish-Sea trunk Dublin Port↔Holyhead (~67 nm) sits at the very edge of the all-electric envelope and is the natural Quanta-LR hybrid corridor as range comes online (H2 2026+), removing charging dependency on the open crossing.

precedents.what: $100M, ~100-vessel electric-hydrofoil network with JIH Global, phased over three years
precedents.why_it_matters: Proves an all-electric foiling network financed and deployed at scale — the platform credibility a greenfield bay market like Dublin needs to launch a brand-new mode.

regulatory_note: Dublin Bay activity engages Dublin Port Company, Dún Laoghaire Harbour (Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council) and the Irish Maritime Administration under the Department of Transport. Much of the inner bay is a UNESCO Biosphere, favouring a zero-emission, low-wash craft over conventional planing boats. As a new mode with little incumbent ferry traffic, the main path is foreshore licensing and pier access rather than displacing operators.
seasonality: A temperate maritime climate gives a long but weather-variable season; summer (May–September) is the leisure peak, while the commuter case runs year-round. Atlantic fronts and the exposed outer bay are the main disruption windows — foiling's stabilised, low-wash ride extends the operable envelope versus a conventional planing boat.
